report.headline: Usage rate projected to drop from 23.5% in the EuroLeague to 18.5% in the NBA, below the league average of 20.0%, while the shooting-efficiency projection carries no information

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 18.5% in the NBA, down from 23.5% in the source EuroLeague season and slightly below the target league's minutes-weighted average of 20.0%.

risks.text: The true shooting percentage projection model performs worse than the trivial league-mean baseline (4.5% vs 4.3% mean absolute error) and should not be treated as informative for this metric.

Despite a raw true shooting percentage of 55.2%, this was actually -0.52 standard deviations below the EuroLeague average that season, suggesting the underlying efficiency was already below peers before any league adjustment.

The 80% prediction interval for usage (13.4%-23.7%) spans nearly the full width of one standard deviation on either side of the NBA average, so any single usage estimate should be treated as imprecise.
The estimate rests on only 61 historical EuroLeague-to-NBA transitions, a thin cohort for generalizing this projection.

strengths.text: Assist rate of 25.4% with 5.285 assists per 75 possessions indicates a significant playmaking role in the source season.
Turnover rate was a low 12.5%, suggesting efficient ball-handling relative to usage.
Source-season usage rate stood at +0.71 standard deviations above the EuroLeague average, marking this as a high-usage offensive role before the move.
38.5% of shot attempts came from three, indicating a shot profile weighted toward floor spacing.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 13.4% to 23.7%, a span of roughly two standard deviations of NBA usage rate (5.2%), and the 95% interval widens to 10.7%-26.4%; the model can rank this player against peers but cannot pin down an individual usage figure, even though it does beat the naive league-mean baseline by 3.2% to 4.2% mean absolute error.
